evidence: M-O s.v. air pressure: āeris pressiō
terms.comment: Classically a technical word of Vitruvius; Traupman and Morgan–Owens use it for blood and air pressure.

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 2.54: dēpellit pressum omnem ponderum

terms.comment: Lewis & Short: post-Augustan; in Pliny, one pressing of grapes or olives.

phrases.latin: ut onera contentīs corporibus facilius feruntur, remissīs opprimunt, simillimē animus intentiōne suā dēpellit pressum omnem ponderum
phrases.english: as loads are carried more easily when the body is braced, and crush it when it is slack, just so the mind, by bracing itself, throws off all the pressure of its burdens

sources: Lewis & Short: pressio · Lewis & Short: pressus · Lewis & Short: pressura
